This bill would update how vocational education and training data is collected, used and shared under the national regulator's act.

It would let the Ministerial Council name another person or body to approve data requirements, and allow the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations' top official to release some training information to the public.
Decisions made by the National VET Regulator to exempt a provider from reporting data under the new rules would not be open to merits review.
Allows the Ministerial Council to designate an alternative person or body to agree to the Data Provision Requirements.
Permits the senior official of the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations to make public certain VET training information, excluding personal details except the training provider's name.
Lets the Secretary issue a determination for collecting, using or disclosing information to build or run a VET data system.
Provides that administrative decisions by the National VET Regulator on data reporting exemptions will not be subject to merits review.
Registered training organisations, students, government policy makers, VET regulators, researchers, employers, and the Australian Skills Quality Authority.

A large majority supported [passing the bill](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2023-06-22.181.1) in the Senate. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to give it a third reading. Since the bill had already passed in the House of Representatives, it will now become law. ### What does the bill do? According to the [explanatory memorandum](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Fems%2Fr6990_ems_d6d1c6b4-b992-45f5-9cca-c3ef8ba9ae08%22;rec=0): > *The purpose of the Bill is to better support data collection and other related measures being implemented as part of the VET Data Streamlining (VDS) reforms.* > > *The Bill seeks to amend the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Act 2011 (the Act) to support data collection and arrangements in relation to the use and disclosure of Vocational Education Training (VET) data and will allow skills ministers to delegate their powers to agree to all, or parts, of the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator ( Data Provision Requirements) Instrument 2020 (the DPRs) to other individuals or bodies, such as senior officials of the Commonwealth and States and Territories.* > > *The amendments will ensure that the information collected from students and training providers, and the data systems being built to facilitate the transfer of that data into the national Vocational Education and Training (VET) data set, are flexible and responsive to the needs of governments and other users of VET data.* Note that the explanatory memorandum is a document that is written by Members of Parliament and not the parliamentary library, so are often biased in favour of the bill they are describing.

The National Vocational Education and Training Regulator (Data Streamlining) Amendment Bill 2023 was introduced to modernise VET data collection, reducing reporting lags of up to 20 months to improve responsiveness to skills shortages. The bill enables streamlined data obligations, authorises ICT system operators to access VET data, and supports 180,000 fee-free TAFE places and the $50 million TAFE Technology Fund.

Bills on financial accountability, financial services compensation, health, national security, education and vocational training were referred to the Federation Chamber for further consideration. The speaker also remarked that they hoped their next speech would be more interesting.

The coalition supported the bill to improve VET data collection but warned against the government's bias towards TAFE over private providers, and criticised Labor's record on VET, including the VET FEE-HELP scheme and insufficient new fee-free TAFE places.

The Selection of Bills Committee report recommended referrals for several bills; an amendment to not refer the Financial Accountability Regime Bill 2023 and related bills was opposed by the Greens, who argued for an inquiry into the Australian Banking Association's influence and the removal of million-dollar fines for bankers.
National Vocational Education and Training Regulator (Data Streamlining) Amendment Act 2023
The bill makes several changes to the Therapeutic Goods Act 1989 to improve safety and oversight of medicines and medical devices.

It would require hospitals to report adverse events involving medical devices, allow imports of substitute prescription medicines during shortages, and expand information-gathering powers for the Health Department Secretary.

The government says seized goods could be retained for 120 days instead of 90, and some therapeutic goods advertising directed at health professionals would no longer need to meet existing advertising restrictions.
Introduces mandatory reporting of adverse events related to medical devices, mainly by hospitals.
Creates a new marketing approval pathway for biologicals intended only for export.
Lets the Secretary approve import or supply of overseas prescription medicines as substitutes for short medicines.
Removes merits review rights for Secretary decisions requiring information or documents.
Enables the Secretary to require anyone to provide documents relevant to possible contraventions of the Act.
Extends from 90 to 120 days the period seized goods may be retained for testing and evidence preparation.
Hospitals, sponsors of medicines and medical devices, health professionals, and government agencies are affected.

Several bills were referred to the Federation Chamber for further consideration, including amendments to private health insurance, therapeutic goods, and export control legislation.

The coalition supported the bill’s measures for mandatory adverse-event reporting by hospitals, a marketing pathway for export-only biologicals, and importation of substitute medicines to address shortages, but raised concerns about removing merits review rights for secretary decisions and called for action on cost-of-living pressures, citing $60 GP consults and $55 scripts.

The Therapeutic Goods Amendment (2022 Measures No. 1) Bill introduces mandatory reporting of adverse events involving medical devices by hospitals, expands information-gathering powers for the health secretary, and creates a streamlined approval pathway for export-only biologicals, aiming to improve patient safety and address medicine shortages.

The speaker supported the Therapeutic Goods Amendment (2022 Measures No. 1) Bill 2022, which introduces mandatory adverse event reporting for hospitals and an export-only pathway for biologicals, but raised concerns about Schedule 10 removing natural justice rights for product sponsors before TGA publication of non-safety information. The speaker also criticised the government over the potential removal of the insulin product FiAsp from the PBS, affecting over 15,000 Australians.

The senator argued that the Therapeutic Goods Amendment (2022 Measures No. 1) Bill 2022 destroys fundamental human rights and legal principles, giving unelected bureaucrats unchecked power over drug approvals, and urged the Senate to vote it down. They specifically opposed provisions removing natural justice, reversing the evidential burden of proof, and creating a backdoor for permanent approval of new drugs without safety testing, and noted the Scrutiny of Bills Committee’s criticisms and 20,000 excess deaths in 2022.

The government moved to amend the Therapeutic Goods Amendment (2022 Measures No. 1) Bill to limit the exclusion of the natural justice hearing rule, allowing its omission only when releasing information that is in the interests of public health or safety or relates to therapeutic goods safety.

Ms Sharkie [explained that](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debate/?id=2022-11-10.26.1): > *The purpose of this amendment is to amend section 23 of the Fair Work Act with the effect of changing the definition of a small business. For most businesses this would mean most, if not all, of their casual the employees would be included in the employee count for the purposes of defining a small business.* > > *My amendment seeks to change the number of employees that define a small business from 15 to 100. The speaker seconded the Restoring Territory Rights Bill 2022, arguing that Australians in the ACT and Northern Territory have been denied the right to debate voluntary assisted dying since the 1997 Andrews bill, and urged parliament to support the bill to restore equal democratic rights.

The speaker moved to suspend standing orders to allow immediate debate on the Restoring Territory Rights Bill 2022, with a two-hour time limit followed by referral to the Federation Chamber until all members have spoken, then return to the House for a vote. He also outlined plans to expedite the Australian Human Rights Commission Legislation Amendment (Selection and Appointment) Bill 2022 and the Treasury Laws Amendment (2022 Measures No. 1) Bill 2022 before question time, and noted a condolence for Archie Roach.

The speaker argued that the Restoring Territory Rights Bill 2022 should pass to restore the ACT and Northern Territory’s power to legislate on euthanasia, a right they held until the Euthanasia Laws Act 1997 removed it. They emphasised that territory citizens deserve the same democratic rights as state citizens, noted the ACT now has over 450,000 residents, and stated their personal opposition to euthanasia while insisting the decision belongs to territory legislatures.

The speaker opposed the Restoring Territory Rights Bill 2022, arguing that territories lack the legislative systems to properly handle euthanasia and that the federal government should address the issue itself rather than devolving power to lower levels of government.

The speaker supported the Restoring Territory Rights Bill 2022, arguing territories should have the same legislative powers as states, including on voluntary assisted dying. The bill repeals section 50A of the Northern Territory (Self-Government) Act without automatically reinstating the Rights of the Terminally Ill Act 1995, and the speaker called for a comprehensive education campaign before any new euthanasia laws.

The speaker opposed the Restoring Territory Rights Bill 2022, arguing it would enable territories to legalise euthanasia and voluntary assisted dying, which he believes violates the sanctity of life and should not be authorised by the federal parliament.

Opposed the Restoring Territory Rights Bill 2022, arguing it is a backdoor attempt to legalise euthanasia in the territories rather than granting them statehood, and referenced a letter from Catholic Archbishop Christopher Prowse.

The speaker opposed the Restoring Territory Rights Bill 2022, arguing that euthanasia legislation is too risky with insufficient safeguards and could undermine palliative care funding, despite supporting the principle of territorial self-determination.

The speaker argued that the Restoring Territory Rights Bill 2022 should be passed to give the ACT and Northern Territory the same right as states to legislate on voluntary assisted dying, citing his own 2010 stage 3 melanoma diagnosis as personal context. He noted that all six states have already passed such laws, making the current ban on territories "incongruous" and "illogical."

The speaker argued for the Restoring Territory Rights Bill 2022, which would remove federal restrictions on the ACT and Northern Territory to legislate on voluntary assisted dying, and stated that territories should have the same self-government as states, while also noting the need for improved palliative care as highlighted in a 2014 Grattan Institute report.

The speaker argued against the Restoring Territory Rights Bill 2022, opposing the legalisation of euthanasia in the Northern Territory and ACT, citing risks to Indigenous Australians, inadequate safeguards given the NT government’s failures, and the slippery slope seen in overseas jurisdictions like the Netherlands and Canada. They noted particular figures: 331 deaths in Victoria’s first two years, 171 in Western Australia by May 2022, and an increase in Oregon from 34 to 134 annual deaths over a decade.

The speaker supported the Restoring Territory Rights Bill 2022, arguing that the ACT and Northern Territory should have the same ability as the states to legislate voluntary assisted dying, based on principles of self-determination and the harm principle. The speaker emphasized that the bill does not mandate new laws, but would allow territory governments to enact their own safe, patient-centered frameworks.
The speaker opposed the Restoring Territory Rights Bill 2022, arguing that no one has the right to kill another person and citing personal experience caring for his father.
Apologised for missing the vote on the Restoring Territory Rights Bill 2022 and affirmed full support for the bill.
